Camera data wrangling

camera-data-wrangling.Rmd

The use of camera traps in ecological studies has become increasingly popular for monitoring wildlife. Managing and analyzing camera trap data efficiently is important for extracting meaningful and accurate insights. In this vignette, we will explore how to perform camera data wrangling, specifically focusing on the ABMI’s Ecosystem Health 2014 data set.

Use the wt_download_report() function to retrieve the main report for the CAM sensor in the Ecosystem Health 2014 project:

eh14_raw <- wt_download_report(
  project_id = 205, 
  sensor_id = "CAM",
  report = "main"
)
head(eh14_raw)
## # A tibble: 6 × 35
##   project_id location location_id latitude longitude location_buffer_m
##        <int> <chr>          <int>    <dbl>     <dbl>             <dbl>
## 1        205 509-NW         47752     56.6     -112.              5500
## 2        205 509-NW         47752     56.6     -112.              5500
## 3        205 509-NW         47752     56.6     -112.              5500
## 4        205 509-NW         47752     56.6     -112.              5500
## 5        205 509-NW         47752     56.6     -112.              5500
## 6        205 509-NW         47752     56.6     -112.              5500
## # ℹ 29 more variables: equipment_serial <chr>, image_id <int>,
## #   image_date_time <dttm>, image_set_id <dbl>, image_fov <chr>,
## #   image_snow <lgl>, image_snow_depth_m <dbl>, image_water_depth_m <dbl>,
## #   species_scientific_name <chr>, species_common_name <chr>,
## #   individual_count <chr>, age_class <chr>, sex_class <chr>, behaviours <chr>,
## #   health_diseases <chr>, coat_colours <chr>, coat_attributes <chr>,
## #   tine_attributes <chr>, direction_travel <chr>, has_collar <lgl>, …

Evaluate independent detections with wt_ind_detect():

# Back to the Ecosystem Health 2014 data.

eh14_detections <- wt_ind_detect(
  x = eh14_raw, 
  threshold = 30,
  units = "minutes",
  remove_human = TRUE, 
  remove_domestic = TRUE 
)
head(eh14_detections, width = 75) 
## # A tibble: 6 × 10
##   detection          project_id location species_common_name start_time         
##   <chr>                   <int> <chr>    <chr>               <dttm>             
## 1 Snowshoe Hare 1           205 509-NW   Snowshoe Hare       2014-03-27 02:10:28
## 2 White-tailed Deer…        205 509-NW   White-tailed Deer   2014-06-20 11:35:08
## 3 Black Bear 1              205 509-SW   Black Bear          2014-06-05 07:30:17
## 4 Canada Lynx 1             205 509-SW   Canada Lynx         2014-04-04 22:19:04
## 5 Gray Wolf 1               205 509-SW   Gray Wolf           2014-04-28 19:04:00
## 6 Grouse, Ptarmigan…        205 509-SW   Grouse, Ptarmigan … 2014-03-25 13:39:12
## # ℹ 5 more variables: end_time <dttm>, total_duration_seconds <dbl>,
## #   n_images <int>, avg_animals_per_image <dbl>, max_animals <dbl>

So there are 313 independent detections in this data set, when using a threshold of 30 minutes.

The output from wt_ind_detect() gave us some useful information. But we probably need to do additional wrangling for our data to be in the proper format for certain modeling techniques (e.g. habitat modeling, occupancy). For example, we want to evaluate the number of detections in a specified time interval (e.g. daily, weekly, or monthly), including zeroes.

Summarise your camera data

With wt_summarise_cam() you can get:

  • The output from wt_ind_detect() (e.g. the object eh14_detections)
  • Your raw data (e.g. the object eh14_raw)
  • The time interval you’re interested in (e.g. weekly)
  • The variable you’re interested in (e.g. detections, presence/absence)
  • The desired output format (‘wide’ or ‘long’)
# A call to `wt_summarise_cam()`:

eh14_summarised <- wt_summarise_cam(
  # Supply your detection data
  detect_data = eh14_detections,
  # Supply your raw image data
  raw_data = eh14_raw,
  # Now specify the time interval you're interested in 
  time_interval = "week",
  # What variable are you interested in?
  variable = "detections",
  # Your desired output format (wide or long) 
  output_format = "wide" 
)
head(eh14_summarised)
## # A tibble: 6 × 24
##   project_id location  year  week n_days_effort `Black Bear` `Canada Lynx`
##        <int> <chr>    <int> <dbl>         <int>        <int>         <int>
## 1        205 509-NW    2014    13             7            0             0
## 2        205 509-NW    2014    14             7            0             0
## 3        205 509-NW    2014    15             7            0             0
## 4        205 509-NW    2014    16             7            0             0
## 5        205 509-NW    2014    17             7            0             0
## 6        205 509-NW    2014    18             7            0             0
## # ℹ 17 more variables: Coyote <int>, `Cranes, Rails, Coots` <int>, Crow <int>,
## #   Deer <int>, `Ducks, Swans, Geese` <int>, Fisher <int>, `Gray Jay` <int>,
## #   `Gray Wolf` <int>, `Grouse, Ptarmigan and allies` <int>, Marten <int>,
## #   Moose <int>, `Red Fox` <int>, `Red Squirrel` <int>, `Snowshoe Hare` <int>,
## #   Songbird <int>, Unidentified <int>, `White-tailed Deer` <int>

Visualize your summaries

The ‘long’ output format works nicely with ggplot2. Below, we summarise species presence in the Ecosystem Health 2014 data at four different time intervals and plot each as a stacked bar chart, coloured by species.

library(ggplot2)

Across the full deployment

Setting time_interval = "full" summarises presence across the entire deployment period for each location:

wt_summarise_cam(
  detect_data = eh14_detections,
  raw_data = eh14_raw,
  time_interval = "full",
  variable = "presence",
  output_format = "long"
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = location, y = value, fill = species_common_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  ylab("Presence") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
         legend.position = "bottom")

By month 

wt_summarise_cam(
  detect_data = eh14_detections,
  raw_data = eh14_raw,
  time_interval = "month",
  variable = "presence",
  output_format = "long"
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = value, fill = species_common_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_classic() +
  ylab("Presence") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.size = unit(0.35, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 7)
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 4, title = NULL))

By week 

wt_summarise_cam(
  detect_data = eh14_detections,
  raw_data = eh14_raw,
  time_interval = "week",
  variable = "presence",
  output_format = "long"
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = value, fill = species_common_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  ylab("Presence") +
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
         legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 4, title = NULL))

By day 

wt_summarise_cam(
  detect_data = eh14_detections,
  raw_data = eh14_raw,
  time_interval = "day",
  variable = "presence",
  output_format = "long") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day, y = value, fill = species_common_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_classic() +
  ylab("Presence") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
         legend.position = "bottom")

And now you can get straight into the science!
